chapter: U Street, Jelly Roll Morton, the youth band and the WPA
title: Taking over the band; stock arrangements and Billy White
summary: Roberts loses interest, the kids carry on buying stock arrangements and copying records, and Billy White writes for them.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: But anyway, this fellow, he had the band and he rehearsed it two or three times, but he never got a job or anything for us. He just sort of (?) rehearsing. Finally I think he kind of lost interest, or maybe some attempts he had made to try to sell it running up against competition with the other more mature bands -- as I said, they had five of them. So with him trying to get a bunch of kids to play somewhere, I guess it probably didn't seem very profitable.
So when he dropped the band, we continued it, and that was when I began my I guess second and real serious stage and trying to arrange. So what we would do, we would buy stock

arrangements. There was a fellow who was an excellent musician, played with Duke Ellington, or wrote music for Duke and everything, and later sort of came to kind of a tragic end... Because as a young man he was very brilliant; I think he graduated from Juilliard. His name was Billy White. He played with Duke briefly in the Forties, and he was the kind of a guy that could have... He was ahead of his time, really, because he could have been an excellent contract musician As a clarinet player, anyone who ever heard him play Classical or... Well, he wasn't too much of a Jazz player, but his Classical...and technique and everything... He also studied with this famous clarinet player with the Marine band. I don't remember what his name was, but he was quite a renowned clarinet player at that particular time.

So this fellow's name was Billy White, and he used to write us some arrangements. And then listening to records, we would pick out things that the bands were playing and try to duplicate them. In the meanwhile, I would get some brilliant idea and I would sit down at the piano, and I would make a chord for somebody and tell each saxophone what to play, then I would make another one and tell the trumpets what to play, and tell the other guys, and then just hit it and see what it sounds like. Then that sounds good, so then I'd give them another chord.
